“Dr. Waldron, Elsie needs help!” Elsie’s husband was adamant, almost angry, as he stared at me. On the other hand, Elsie stared at the floor, almost as though she wasn’t present. I had never met either of the couple before and was struggling just a little to figure out what was needed from me to help her.

“What is going on?” I asked as I flipped through her chart. This was still in the days of paper charts, and I headed to the lab section of her chart. There wasn’t anything too crazy that I could see there—her liver enzymes were a little elevated, but otherwise, everything seemed OK.

“It’s her drinking!” Her husband told me. “She is drinking more and more every night. She won’t go out except to get whiskey. She drinks till she passes out every night and has to have something every morning to get her started.”

“Is that true?” I asked Elsie, feeling like a judge overseeing a jury trial.

“Yes,” she said. Her face was emotionless, and I couldn’t tell if she wanted to be there or not.

“Do you want help?” I asked her. This was a loaded question. Many people who struggle with alcoholism aren’t ready to break free from its vice-like hold on them. Maybe Elsie was different.

“I guess so,” she said, indifferently. Once again, I couldn’t tell whether she wanted to be there or not.

“At the rate at which you are drinking, you will kill yourself within a year – maybe two at best – if you don’t give up alcohol entirely,” I told her. “If you want to, I will try to find you an inpatient program to detox you and get you off of alcohol.”

“She’s ready,” he husband said firmly.

When dealing with someone who drinks heavily, it is crucial that they don’t simply stop drinking without medical support. Abrupt cessation of alcohol use causes the body to go into withdrawal which can produce a state called Delirium Tremens and even seizures.

I stepped out of the exam room and to make phone calls. It is never easy to find a place for someone to attempt to rehabilitate from any kind of substances, and it was over an hour and a half before I found a facility that was willing to take Elsie and try to help her get off of the whiskey.

I sighed as I reentered her exam room. I had been afraid that I wouldn’t find anywhere for her to go.

I told them about the plan, and her husband nodded vigorously, while Elise continued to stare silently at the floor. “Can we pray together before you go?” I asked them, and when they nodded assent, I prayed with them, asking for freedom and Jesus’ presence in both of their lives.

They left my office with marching orders and directions on where to go. I had a happy glow about me for the rest of the morning, knowing that I had gone the extra mile and had really made a difference in this middle-aged couple’s life.

Around 2 pm, I got a call from the rehab facility. They hadn’t seen even a shadow of Elsie or her husband, which was surprising, since it was a bright sunny day and the facility wasn’t that far away. With a sinking feeling, I dialed the couple’s phone number.

“She won’t go!” Her husband told me. “She tells me that she told me this ahead of time. She’ll try to cut back, but she isn’t willing to go into a rehab facility or any such thing. I guess just tell them that we’ll let them know if she changes her mind.”

My nurse called the rehab facility and told them the bad news, and I sat down in my chair, stunned. What else could I have done? Was there a solution for Elsie—something different that I could have said that would have made a difference in her life?

About a year later, I received the sad news that Elsie had died at home. I was certain that things would have been different if she had gone to rehab and if she had given control to Jesus. None of that had happened, and I felt cynicism pushing into my heart.

Cynicism

We live in an age of cynicism. In ancient Greece, the cynics were an odd assortment of men who specialized in being grouchy and saying mean (they would have said truthful) things to people. They often dressed in rags and behaved in such a way that most of the polite Athenians did not want to be close to them.

Today, cynicism means a tendency to believe the worst about people and circumstances. Cynical people believe that all people are motivated purely by selfishness and that bad events will tend to prevail.

Many young doctors are idealistic and very hopeful. They believe that if they exert the utmost effort, they can make a real, positive impact on their patient’s lives. Unfortunately, as time goes by and they try their hardest and their patients don’t change, they can give up. These doctors still try, but they no longer really hope that their efforts will make much of a difference.

It seems as though people who get involved with politics often have the best of intentions. They see this as a path to changing society for the better. Unfortunately, as time goes by and the faces in charge change, the policies don’t really change, they tend to become cynical.

Sometimes this cynicism is directed against all politicians. Sometimes it is only anger directed against members of the party that opposes their party’s positions. Hope is replaced by cynicism.

Cynicism in the Bible

If there is a book in the Bible that seems to have been written by a cynical man, it is the book of Ecclesiastes. The Preacher, who we understand to be Solomon, lists all of the things that he endeavored in an attempt to find joy.

In chapter 2:17-23 Solomon describes work as futile. He finishes by saying, “For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun? For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity.” (Ecclesiastes 2:22,23)

He saw the world as being dominated by tyrants and there was little that the people could do about it. Solomon went so far as to say that political power was meaningless “Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished. For out of prison he cometh to reign; whereas also he that is born in his kingdom becometh poor” (Ecclesiastes 4:13).

In Ecclesiastes 6:6, he seems to disparage long life. “Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?”

Of course, he finishes his short book with the instruction to remember our Creator in the days of our youth. There is a blessing for those who choose to focus on God when they have a little bit of energy left and not, when they are old and jaded, like Solomon.

Later on, it almost seemed as though God had given up on His people. He still sent prophets to them, but He knew without a doubt that the people would refuse to respond. “Therefore thou shalt speak all these words unto them; but they will not hearken to thee: thou shalt also call unto them; but they will not answer thee” (Jeremiah 7:27).

Even in the New Testament, Paul told Timothy that the time was coming when people would no longer listen to sound doctrine. “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;” (2 Timothy 4:3).

By picking and choosing these passages, we can come away with a very gloomy view of the future and, more specifically, of human’s willingness to change. It seems there is little point of investing ourselves in the people around us. They are full of woe and are as likely to change as a chipmunk is to master differential calculus.

The Opposite of Cynicism

The opposite of cynicism is hope. It is the belief that the future could be better.

It is interesting that the Apostle Paul spoke of tribulations in the Epistle to the Romans, “And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope: and hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us” (Romans 5:3-5).

We may not have reached the place where we glory in the trials we experience, but certainly, they should bring us these other things that he mentions. For, we grow in patience and experience, even as we deal with trials, but more than that, we come to realize that we have hope for tomorrow because we serve a great God.

The contrast in the story of the Prodigal Son in Luke 15 teaches us much about hope. The father and the older brother were strikingly different in their attitudes.

The father had never given up hope – he knew that his son had failed him and gone far from what he knew was right and yet, the father still desired to see the prodigal come to himself and return home.

On the other hand, the older brother not only had no hope for his younger brother, but he was also angry with him. The prodigal had wasted his money, he had lived in sin, and now, he had returned home just because he was out of money.

Certainly, there was no reason to trust the younger son. Yet, that is exactly what our Heavenly Father does for us.

Look for Hope in the Right Places

Part of the problem is that we look for hope in the wrong places. A number of years ago, a presidential candidate ran for office under the slogan “Hope and Change,” and yet, even though he was elected, I imagine most folks did not feel that their lives were significantly changed for the better.

Pursuing the things this world values—political power and wealth is guaranteed to bring emptiness. This is Satan’s pattern—he always over-promises and under-delivers.

This was what he did when he tempted Jesus, “All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:8). All of the things Satan offered, nothing compared with the glory that Jesus eventually received from the road that led to the cross.

In the same way, Satan would like to distract Christians from seeking the things that are valuable, and that will bring hope. Satan tells Christians that politics will not only change the world for the better, it is an easier way to change the world.

The Bible is clear that we build hope as we nurture our relationship with God and then work to help our brothers and sisters build that same relationship in their own lives. The reason that we can hope is not because people are so wonderful—we don’t have to live very long to realize that they aren’t. The reason we hope is because we serve an awesome, faithful God who walks with us through the worst of our trials.

Remember that We Have Undeserved Hope

Jesus’ messages about forgiveness make it clear that one of the major reasons that we have for forgiving others in our lives is that we have received great and undeserved forgiveness. The same is true for hope.

Each one of us was hopeless and without reason to expect to receive hope and we were still given a ray of light in the midst of our darkness. Maybe part of the reason that we have so much trouble hoping for good things for the people around us is that we do not remember how hopeless we were before we found grace.

If Jesus was able to bring hope to our hopeless existence, then certainly He can do wonderful things in the hearts and lives of others around us. The only people we should give up on are the ones that our Savior has given up on as well.

Small Efforts Do Make a Difference

I remember having a conversation with a young person who was planning to go into medicine and had a plan to go to a foreign country and serve the people there. As we were talking, an older man entered the conversation and shared that he saw little hope for change in developing countries.

The people in those countries just weren’t interested in getting better and didn’t do the minimum necessary to stave off things like worms and parasites. Doctors and nurses couldn’t make a difference in such an environment.

I could sense the heart of the youth sinking as this older man shared. He had experience, and he had given up hope. The sad thing was that he was also stealing the hope of someone who still had a desire to serve.

When I was in training, I had a surgeon tell me that family doctors didn’t really do anything. They simply kept their patients alive till their next office visit, whereas surgeons really “fixed” people—taking out (or off) the offending body part.

At the end of the day, small efforts do make a difference. I don’t do brain surgery, but I still can make a difference in someone else’s life— maybe just by spending a little time and listening and praying. This is true for all of us.

More than that, we come to realize that making this effort changes our own lives for the better. Jesus told the sheep that as they ministered to “the least of these my brethren,” they were ministering to Him.

Even if no one’s life is improved, our Savior knows our desires and feels our efforts, and will reward them someday.

A Few Things to Remember

When we face failures, we tend to move in one of two directions. Those of us who are optimists tend to believe that this episode was an isolated event and that the future is still bright. On the other hand, pessimists believe that failures are permanent, personal, and pervasive.

Pessimists believe that their failures are the result of intrinsic character flaws that they have and that these things affect all of their lives and are unlikely to change. Unlike the righteous man who falls to rise again, these people fall and lie where they fall, defeated at the outset.

When we are dealing with other people, we need to give them the same grace that we should give ourselves. They, too, are growing, and if they have a failure today, they will do better tomorrow. Maybe they will fail again, but they will at least “fail better.”

Conclusion

Cynicism is rife in our world. Many have given up hope for a better future, and it is understandable for those who have invested their hope in this world’s institutions. There is no real hope in government or in armies or in bureaucracy.

The song says, “Oh to have no hope in Jesus, how dark this world must be!” For, Jesus is the one who brings light into our darkness and allows us to continue, even when others fail us.

God is the one who redeems us. He is the one who sent the prophets, even though their messages were ignored, and the prophets were persecuted. He is the one who continues to hope for us, even when we have failed Him so many times in the past.

He is the reason we carry on. He is the reason that we have hope, not only for ourselves but also for our brothers.

“Dr. Waldron, Elsie heeft hulp nodig!” Elsie’s man was vastberaden, bijna boos, terwijl hij naar me staarde. Elsie daarentegen staarde naar de vloer, bijna alsof ze er niet bij was. Ik had het paar nog nooit eerder ontmoet en probeerde een beetje te achterhalen wat er van mij werd verwacht om haar te helpen.

“Wat is er aan de hand?” vroeg ik terwijl ik door haar dossier bladerde. Dit was nog in de tijd van papieren dossiers, en ik ging naar het laboratoriumgedeelte van haar kaart. Daar zag ik niets al te geks—haar leverenzymen waren iets verhoogd, maar verder leek alles in orde.

“Het is haar drank!” vertelde haar man me. “Ze drinkt steeds meer elke avond. Ze gaat nergens heen behalve om whisky te halen. Ze drinkt tot ze flauwvalt elke nacht en moet elke ochtend iets hebben om op gang te komen.”

“Is dat waar?” vroeg ik aan Elsie, me voelend als een rechter die een juryproces leidt.

“Ja,” zei ze. Haar gezicht was emotieloos, en ik kon niet zien of ze daar wilde zijn of niet.

“Wil je hulp?” vroeg ik haar. Dit was een beladen vraag. Veel mensen die worstelen met alcoholisme zijn niet klaar om zich te bevrijden uit die verstikkende greep. Misschien was Elsie anders.

“Ik denk het wel,” zei ze onverschillig. Weer kon ik niet bepalen of ze daar wilde zijn of niet.

“Als je blijft drinken zoals je nu doet, maak je jezelf binnen een jaar—misschien twee in het beste geval—dood, als je niet helemaal stopt met alcohol,” zei ik haar. “Als je wilt, zal ik proberen een opnameprogramma voor je te vinden om te ontgiften en je van de alcohol af te helpen.”

“Ze is er klaar voor,” zei de man beslist.

Als je met iemand te maken hebt die veel drinkt, is het cruciaal dat die persoon niet simpelweg stopt zonder medische ondersteuning. Plotse stopzetting van alcoholgebruik zorgt ervoor dat het lichaam ontwenningsverschijnselen krijgt, wat een toestand kan veroorzaken die Delirium Tremens heet en zelfs toevallen kan opleveren.

Ik stapte de spreekkamer uit om telefoontjes te plegen. Het is nooit gemakkelijk een plek te vinden waar iemand kan proberen te revalideren van welk middel dan ook, en het duurde anderhalf uur voordat ik een instelling vond die bereid was Elsie op te nemen en te helpen van de whisky af te komen.

Ik zuchtte toen ik haar spreekkamer weer binnenkwam. Ik had gevreesd dat ik nergens een plek voor haar zou vinden.

Ik vertelde hen over het plan, en haar man knikte krachtig, terwijl Elsie stil bleef naar de vloer staren. “Kunnen we bidden voordat je weggaat?” vroeg ik, en toen ze instemden, bad ik met hen en vroeg om bevrijding en de aanwezigheid van Jezus in beider levens.

Ze verlieten mijn kantoor met opdrachten en aanwijzingen waar ze heen moesten. Ik had de rest van de ochtend een gelukkig gevoel, wetend dat ik een extra stap had gezet en echt een verschil had gemaakt in het leven van dit middelbare echtpaar.

Rond 14:00 kreeg ik een telefoontje van de revalidatie-instelling. Ze hadden niet eens een schim van Elsie of haar man gezien, wat verrassend was, omdat het een heldere zonnige dag was en de instelling niet zo ver weg lag. Met een zwaar gevoel belde ik het telefoonnummer van het paar.

“Ze wil niet gaan!” vertelde haar man me. “Ze zegt dat ze me dit van tevoren had verteld. Ze zal proberen te minderen, maar ze is niet bereid naar een revalidatie-instelling of iets dergelijks te gaan. Ik denk dat je ze maar moet vertellen dat we het laten weten als ze van gedachten verandert.”

Mijn verpleegkundige belde de revalidatie-instelling om het slechte nieuws te vertellen, en ik ging in mijn stoel zitten, verbijsterd. Wat had ik nog meer kunnen doen? Was er een oplossing voor Elsie—iets anders dat ik had kunnen zeggen dat een verschil in haar leven zou hebben gemaakt?

Ongeveer een jaar later kreeg ik het droevige nieuws dat Elsie thuis was overleden. Ik was ervan overtuigd dat het anders had gelopen als ze naar revalidatie was gegaan en als ze de controle aan Jezus had overgegeven. Niets van dat alles was gebeurd, en ik voelde cynisme in mijn hart opkomen.

Cynisme

We leven in een tijd van cynisme. In het oude Griekenland waren de cynici een vreemde verzameling mannen die gespecialiseerd waren in knorrig zijn en nare (zij zouden zeggen waarheidsgetrouwe) dingen tegen mensen zeggen. Ze droegen vaak lompen en gedroegen zich zodanig dat de meeste beleefde Atheneren niet in hun nabijheid wilden zijn.

Tegenwoordig betekent cynisme een neiging het ergste van mensen en omstandigheden te geloven. Cynische mensen denken dat alle mensen uitsluitend door eigenbelang worden gedreven en dat slechte gebeurtenissen de overhand zullen krijgen.

Veel jonge artsen zijn idealistisch en vol hoop. Ze geloven dat als ze zich maximaal inspannen, ze een echt, positief verschil in het leven van hun patiënten kunnen maken. Helaas, na verloop van tijd, wanneer zij hun best doen en hun patiënten niet veranderen, kunnen ze opgeven. Deze artsen proberen het nog wel, maar ze hopen niet meer echt dat hun inzet veel zal uitmaken.

Het lijkt alsof mensen die zich met politiek bemoeien vaak de beste bedoelingen hebben. Ze zien dit als een weg om de samenleving ten goede te veranderen. Helaas, na verloop van tijd en als de gezichten aan de macht veranderen maar de beleidslijnen niet echt veranderen, neigen ze ernaar cynisch te worden.

Soms is dit cynisme gericht tegen alle politici. Soms is het alleen woede gericht tegen leden van de partij die tegenover hen staat. Hoop wordt vervangen door cynisme.

Cynisme in de Bijbel

Als er een boek in de Bijbel is dat geschreven lijkt te zijn door een cynische man, is het het boek Prediker. De Prediker, die wij begrijpen als Salomo, somt alles op wat hij ondernomen heeft in een poging vreugde te vinden.

In hoofdstuk 2:17-23 beschrijft Salomo arbeid als vergeefs. Hij eindigt met de woorden: “Want wat heeft de mens aan al zijn arbeid, en aan de benauwdheid van zijn hart, waardoor hij gewerkt heeft onder de zon? Want al zijn dagen zijn smarten, en zijn arbeid verdriet; ja, zijn hart rust niet des nachts. Dit is ook ijdelheid.” (Prediker 2:22,23)

Hij zag de wereld gedomineerd door tirannen en er was weinig dat het volk ertegen kon doen. Salomo ging zo ver te zeggen dat politieke macht zinloos was: “Beter is een arm en wijs kind dan een oud en dwaas koning, die niet meer berispt zal worden. Want uit de gevangenis gaat hij om te regeren; en hij die geboren is in zijn koninkrijk wordt arm.” (Prediker 4:13).

In Prediker 6:6 lijkt hij een lang leven te kleineren. “Ja, al leefde hij duizend jaar tweemaal verteld, toch heeft hij geen goed gezien: gaan zij niet allen naar één plaats?”

Natuurlijk eindigt hij zijn korte boek met de aansporing onze Schepper te gedenken in de dagen van onze jeugd. Er is een zegen voor degenen die ervoor kiezen zich op God te richten wanneer ze nog wat energie over hebben en niet, zoals Salomo, als ze oud en verbitterd zijn.

Later leek het bijna alsof God Zijn volk had opgegeven. Hij zond nog profeten naar hen, maar Hij wist zonder twijfel dat het volk zou weigeren te reageren. “Daarom zult gij al deze woorden tot hen spreken; maar zij zullen niet naar u horen: ook zult gij tot hen roepen; maar zij zullen u niet antwoorden.” (Jeremia 7:27).

Zelfs in het Nieuwe Testament vertelde Paulus aan Timoteüs dat de tijd zou komen dat mensen geen gezonde leer meer zouden verdragen. “Want er zal een tijd zijn, dat zij de gezonde leer niet zullen verdragen; maar naar hun eigen begeerten zullen zij zich leraren verzamelen, die zich horen krabben;” (2 Timoteüs 4:3).

Door deze passages uit te kiezen en te combineren, kunnen we een zeer sombere kijk op de toekomst en, specifieker, op de bereidheid van mensen om te veranderen overhouden. Het lijkt weinig zinvol om ons in te zetten voor de mensen om ons heen. Ze zijn vol ellende en zo waarschijnlijk te veranderen als een eekhoorn differentiaalrekening te beheersen.

Het tegengestelde van cynisme

Het tegengestelde van cynisme is hoop. Het is het geloof dat de toekomst beter kan zijn.

Het is interessant dat de apostel Paulus over verdrukkingen sprak in de brief aan de Romeinen: “En niet alleen dat, maar wij roemen ook in verdrukkingen; wetende dat verdrukking volharding werkt; en volharding ervaring; en ervaring hoop; en hoop maakt niet beschaamd; omdat de liefde Gods uitgestort is in onze harten door de Heilige Geest, die ons gegeven is” (Romeinen 5:3-5).

Misschien zijn we er nog niet aan toe gekomen te roemen in de beproevingen die we meemaken, maar zeker zouden die ons de andere dingen moeten brengen die hij noemt. Want we groeien in volharding en ervaring, zelfs terwijl we met beproevingen omgaan, en meer dan dat, we komen tot het besef dat we hoop voor morgen hebben omdat we een grote God dienen.

Het contrast in het verhaal van de Verloren Zoon in Lukas 15 leert ons veel over hoop. De vader en de oudere broer waren opvallend verschillend in hun houdingen.

De vader had nooit de hoop opgegeven—hij wist dat zijn zoon hem had teleurgesteld en ver van het juiste was afgedwaald, en toch verlangde de vader nog steeds dat de verlorene tot inkeer zou komen en terug naar huis zou keren.

De oudere broer daarentegen had niet alleen geen hoop voor zijn jongere broer, hij was ook boos op hem. De verlorene had zijn geld verkwist, had in zonde geleefd, en nu was hij naar huis teruggekomen gewoon omdat hij zonder geld zat.

Er was zeker geen reden om de jongere zoon te vertrouwen. Toch is dat precies wat onze Hemelse Vader voor ons doet.

Zoek hoop op de juiste plekken

Een deel van het probleem is dat we hoop op de verkeerde plaatsen zoeken. Een aantal jaren geleden voerde een presidentskandidaat campagne onder de slogan “Hope and Change,” en toch, hoewel hij gekozen werd, stel ik me voor dat de meeste mensen niet voelden dat hun leven wezenlijk ten goede veranderd was.

Het nastreven van de dingen die deze wereld waardeert—politieke macht en rijkdom—brengt gegarandeerd leegheid. Dit is het patroon van Satan—hij doet altijd te veel beloften en levert te weinig.

Dit deed hij toen hij Jezus verzocht: “Al deze dingen zal ik u geven, als gij neervalt en mij aanbidt” (Mattheüs 4:8). Van al wat Satan aanbood, stond niets in verhouding tot de heerlijkheid die Jezus uiteindelijk ontving door de weg die naar het kruis leidde.

Op dezelfde manier probeert Satan christenen af te leiden van het zoeken naar waardevolle dingen die hoop brengen. Satan vertelt christenen dat politiek de wereld niet alleen ten goede zal veranderen, maar ook dat het een gemakkelijkere manier is om de wereld te veranderen.

De Bijbel maakt duidelijk dat we hoop opbouwen terwijl we onze relatie met God koesteren en daarna werken om onze broeders en zusters te helpen diezelfde relatie in hun leven op te bouwen. De reden dat we hoop kunnen hebben is niet omdat mensen zo geweldig zijn—we hoeven niet lang te leven om te beseffen dat ze dat niet zijn. De reden dat we hoop hebben, is omdat we een geweldige, trouwe God dienen die met ons wandelt door het ergste van onze beproevingen.

Onverdiende hoop herinneren

Jezus’ boodschappen over vergeving maken duidelijk dat een van de belangrijkste redenen om anderen in ons leven te vergeven is dat wij grote en onverdiende vergeving hebben ontvangen. Hetzelfde geldt voor hoop.

Elk van ons was hopeloos en had geen reden te verwachten hoop te ontvangen, en toch kregen we een straaltje licht te midden van onze duisternis. Misschien is een deel van de reden dat we zoveel moeite hebben om goede dingen voor de mensen om ons heen te hopen, dat we niet herinneren hoe hopeloos we waren voordat we genade vonden.

Als Jezus hoop in ons hopeloze bestaan kon brengen, dan kan Hij zeker ook wonderlijke dingen doen in de harten en levens van anderen om ons heen. De enige mensen op wie we zouden moeten opgeven, zijn degenen waarop onze Redder ook opgegeven heeft.

Kleine inspanningen maken wél verschil

Ik herinner me een gesprek met een jong persoon die van plan was geneeskunde te gaan studeren en het plan had naar een vreemd land te gaan om de mensen daar te dienen. Terwijl we praatten, kwam er een oudere man in het gesprek en deelde dat hij weinig hoop op verandering in ontwikkelingslanden zag.

De mensen in die landen waren gewoon niet geïnteresseerd om beter te worden en deden niet het minimum dat nodig was om dingen als wormen en parasieten tegen te gaan. Artsen en verpleegkundigen konden in zo’n omgeving geen verschil maken.

Ik merkte het hart van de jongere zakken terwijl deze oudere man deelde. Hij had ervaring en hij had de hoop opgegeven. Het trieste was dat hij ook de hoop afpakte van iemand die nog een verlangen had om te dienen.

Toen ik in opleiding was, vertelde een chirurg mij dat huisartsen eigenlijk niets deden. Ze hielden hun patiënten gewoon in leven tot het volgende bezoek, terwijl chirurgen echt mensen “herstelden”—door het storende lichaamsdeel te verwijderen (of af te snijden).

Aan het eind van de dag maken kleine inspanningen wél een verschil. Ik doe geen hersenchirurgie, maar ik kan toch een verschil maken in iemands leven—misschien gewoon door wat tijd te nemen en te luisteren en te bidden. Dat geldt voor ons allemaal.

Meer nog, we beseffen dat het ondernemen van deze inspanning ons eigen leven ten goede verandert. Jezus zei tegen de schapen dat toen zij dienden aan “de minste van deze mijn broeders,” zij Hem dienden.

Zelfs als iemands leven niet verbetert, kent onze Redder onze verlangens en voelt Hij onze inspanningen, en zal Hij die op een dag belonen.

Enkele dingen om te onthouden

Wanneer we te maken krijgen met mislukkingen, neigen we een van twee richtingen op te gaan. Wij die optimisten zijn, geloven vaak dat deze episode een geïsoleerd voorval was en dat de toekomst nog steeds helder is. Pessimisten daarentegen geloven dat mislukkingen permanent, persoonlijk en alomvattend zijn.

Pessimisten geloven dat hun mislukkingen het gevolg zijn van intrinsieke karaktergebreken die zij hebben en dat deze dingen al hun leven beïnvloeden en onwaarschijnlijk zullen veranderen. In tegenstelling tot de rechtvaardige die valt om weer op te staan, vallen deze mensen en blijven waar ze gevallen zijn, bij voorbaat verslagen.

Als we met andere mensen omgaan, moeten we hen dezelfde genade geven die we onszelf zouden moeten geven. Ook zij groeien, en als ze vandaag falen, zullen ze het morgen beter doen. Misschien zullen ze opnieuw falen, maar in ieder geval zullen ze “beter falen.”

Conclusie

Cynisme is wijdverbreid in onze wereld. Velen hebben de hoop op een betere toekomst opgegeven, en het is begrijpelijk voor degenen die hun hoop in de instellingen van deze wereld hebben gelegd. Er is geen echte hoop in regering of legers of bureaucratie.

Het lied zegt: “Och, geen hoop op Jezus hebben, hoe donker moet deze wereld dan zijn!” Want Jezus is degene die licht brengt in onze duisternis en ons in staat stelt door te gaan, zelfs wanneer anderen ons laten vallen.

God is degene die ons verlost. Hij is degene die de profeten zond, hoewel hun boodschappen genegeerd werden en de profeten vervolgd werden. Hij is degene die blijf hopen voor ons, zelfs wanneer we Hem zo vaak in het verleden hebben teleurgesteld.

Hij is de reden dat we doorgaan. Hij is de reden dat we hoop hebben, niet alleen voor onszelf maar ook voor onze broeders.

Do you believe in miracles? Do you believe in the supernatural? What about divine intervention? Or a better question might be, have you seen God working in your life? Do others see God working in your life?

My brother was working in the greenhouse when a customer walked in and marveled at the beauty of all the plants. He then exclaimed how impressed he was at all our hard work. My brother responded with, “Some plant, some water, but God gives the increase.” To which the customer responded with, “No, no, don’t give the credit to God. You came out here and did all this work. You planted, watered, and fertilized all these plants, and you all deserve the credit, not God!” The reason the man felt this way is because he was a humanist.

What is Humanism?

The dictionary defines humanism like this; an outlook or system of thought attaching prime importance to human rather than divine or supernatural matters. Humanist beliefs stress the potential value and goodness of human beings, emphasize common human needs, and seek solely rational ways of solving human problems.

If God does exist, then we will have to recognize this fact and answer to Him. Humanists attempt to prove that God does not exist, so they can freely live their lives as they please. According to humanism, there is no God. If so, then we, the human race, are superior to God. Everything is for us and our ultimate happiness. This is the definition of humanism.

Two Types of Humanism

There are two types of humanistic beliefs, and we will look at both. The first belief is the theory that there is no God. In reality, this seems to be the only rational way to be a humanist. Everything is created by man and for man. There are no other factors or supernatural involvement. Everything happens by reason and common sense. There is a logical explanation for everything that happens. Of course, some things do not make sense, but humanists brush those aside and look only at the things that can be explained. Like the plants in the greenhouse, they look at all that man does and ignore the supernatural part of a plant springing forth with new life. Scientists around the world are working diligently to put human reasoning into everything that has ever happened, even the creation of the world. Scientists, with all their learning and wisdom, attempt to give logical explanations for why natural disasters and global crises happen. If they can explain everything, then they can rule out God and His existence. This allows the human race to do as it pleases without eternal consequences. This, in turn leads to a great sense of false peace.

The humanists, with all their reasoning, mock the very existence of God. If you go to most colleges in America and talk to people about Christianity, they laugh at you and mock the fact that Christians actually believe in God.

The second type of humanistic belief is a theory of humanism that acknowledges the existence of God. One anthropologist argued that humanism is a project of modernity and a secularized continuation of Western Christian theology. But if you ask people what they think humanism means, you will likely get different responses, and it becomes very confusing. But why the confusion? Because people are trying to be Christian humanists. Christian Humanism has frequently been criticized for its vagueness and difficulty to define. The reason it has become so confusing is that people want to believe in God but also believe in themselves and that the world revolves around them.

In Romans, we read, “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness; Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them. For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse: Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened. Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things. Wherefore God also gave them up to uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts, to dishonour their own bodies between themselves: Who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen. For this cause God gave them up unto vile affections: for even their women did change the natural use into that which is against nature: And likewise also the men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their lust one toward another; men with men working that which is unseemly, and receiving in themselves that recompence of their error which was meet. And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient; Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers, Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents, Without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful: Who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them” (Romans 1:18-32).

So how can one be a humanist and believe in God? This is where we hit a little closer to home. This type of humanist believes God wants him to be happy. He believes in a Creator God but does not believe he has to serve Him In reality. He doesn’t believe in the true God but, in his mind, created a fictitious god that does not exist. This allows him to live for himself and his own happiness. This type of person will talk about God, go to church, sing songs, and say prayers. However, he will look only to man for all his needs. If he is sick, he calls a doctor. If he needs money, he goes to the banker. If the need is a break from reality, he takes a vacation or retreat. He lives life for his own happiness and then thanks God though he did not look to God for his needs. These people are dependent on themselves. They have confidence in themselves.

Here is an example: A Christian plants a garden and takes care of it each day. He waters and fertilizes weeds and prunes. Finally, his plants all begin to bear fruit, nice fruit. He thanks God for the plentiful harvest. His neighbor, an atheistic humanist, also planted a garden. He, too, went out each day and watered, pruned, weeded, and fertilized. He also received a bountiful harvest. This man, however, boasted of all that he had accomplished. Both men did the same things and had similar results. One gave God the credit, and one credited himself. He will say he accomplished the same thing without God that his neighbor did with God. Christians know that he is wrong and that he actually did need God to grow his garden.

When something happens that requires supernatural intervention, the Christian humanist prays and asks others to pray. However, he does not believe God will answer their prayers and instantly gets to work to solve his problem, with only human reasoning. Then, if the problem is resolved, he thanks God for it. This type of humanism has confused the modern world. It has caused unbelievers to mock the Christian faith and to call it a false religion with no power.

The Christian does not believe in human reasoning. The Christian believes that the God of heaven is the reason for everything. “For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him” (Colossians 1:16). We are nothing without Him, and without Him, we can do nothing. Christianity is the opposite of humanism. When the Christian does something supernatural, something the humanist or atheist cannot do, then we have something that will confound the wise.

When the neighbor sees the Christian loving his enemies, forgiving someone who wronged him, and doing things that he cannot do, he then begins to wonder where the power to do these things came from. This then leads him to the Father. When there is nothing supernatural that we are doing, he is confused.

What About Us?

I fear that we are falling into this trap of ‘Christian Humanism.’ We talk the talk; we say we believe in God. We go to church, sing songs, and say prayers. However, from outward appearances, we trust in ourselves. Because we have centered our lives around ourselves and our well-being, the God of heaven does not hear us. Our prayers are not answered, and the time on our knees is a struggle at best. We go through the motions because that is how we’ve been taught, but our faith lies in human reasoning.

It can be extremely difficult to seek the Lord while living in a humanistic society. A society that has perfected the pursuit of liberty and happiness. Slowly, the church is caving to the ways of this world.

A minister from China was visiting the churches in America. Before departing back to China, he was asked what impressed him most about the churches in America. He replied, “I am amazed at what all they have accomplished without God.”

We would do well to simplify the modern definition of humanism. The humanist proudly denies that there is a God when he boasts of his own strength and abilities. He proclaims the great accomplishments of man and mocks the humble Christian.

The Christian denies himself, picks up his cross, and follows his Master. The Christian thinks nothing of himself or the ability of man, confidently admitting that he is merely dust and back to that dust he will quickly go. The Christian looks for the good in others and trusts God for all his daily needs and cares.

Christians believe they are merely servants to their master. They are hated by the world and despised by most, rejected. “If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you. (John 15:18)” To them, this life is not the pursuit of happiness. The things of this world do not even interest them. Their joy and peace comes solely from serving their master, from pleasing their Heavenly Father. To the world, they are strange. Fools. To God, they are His dear children.

God is still looking for people today who will put their trust in Him. He is looking over all the earth for someone, somewhere, who will put aside human reasoning and common sense and obey the voice from heaven. God wants men with faith who will step out into the supernatural, like Abraham, Moses, David, and the thousands of believers that followed. Someone who will deny himself and this world and follow the Savior.

When this life is over, the humanists, whether they say they believe in God or not, will perish. And the Christians will go on to live forever in glory.

Humanist? Christian? Christian Humanist? Which one are you?

Croyez-vous aux miracles ? Croyez-vous au surnaturel ? Qu'en est-il de l'intervention divine ? Ou une meilleure question serait : avez-vous vu Dieu agir dans votre vie ? Les autres voient-ils Dieu agir dans votre vie ?

Mon frère travaillait dans la serre lorsqu'un client est entré et s'est émerveillé de la beauté de toutes les plantes. Il déclara ensuite combien il était impressionné par tout notre travail. Mon frère répondit : « Quelques plantes, un peu d'eau, mais c'est Dieu qui donne l'accroissement. » Le client répliqua : « Non, non, ne donnez pas le mérite à Dieu. Vous êtes sorti ici et avez fait tout ce travail. Vous avez planté, arrosé et fertilisé toutes ces plantes, et c'est vous qui méritez le mérite, pas Dieu ! » La raison pour laquelle cet homme pensait ainsi, c'est qu'il était humaniste.

Qu'est-ce que l'humanisme ?

Le dictionnaire définit l'humanisme ainsi : une vision ou un système de pensée accordant une importance primordiale aux choses humaines plutôt qu'aux choses divines ou surnaturelles. Les croyances humanistes soulignent la valeur et la bonté potentielles des êtres humains, mettent l'accent sur les besoins humains communs et cherchent des moyens purement rationnels de résoudre les problèmes humains.

Si Dieu existe, alors nous devrons reconnaître ce fait et Lui rendre compte. Les humanistes tentent de prouver que Dieu n'existe pas, afin de pouvoir vivre librement comme bon leur semble. Selon l'humanisme, il n'y a pas de Dieu. Si tel est le cas, alors nous, la race humaine, sommes supérieurs à Dieu. Tout est pour nous et notre bonheur ultime. Telle est la définition de l'humanisme.

Deux types d'humanisme

Il existe deux types de croyances humanistes, et nous examinerons les deux. La première croyance est la théorie selon laquelle il n'y a pas de Dieu. En réalité, cela semble être la seule façon rationnelle d'être humaniste. Tout est créé par l'homme et pour l'homme. Il n'y a pas d'autres facteurs ni d'intervention surnaturelle. Tout se produit par la raison et le bon sens. Il y a une explication logique pour tout ce qui arrive. Bien sûr, certaines choses n'ont pas de sens, mais les humanistes écartent celles-ci et ne regardent que les choses pouvant être expliquées. Comme les plantes dans la serre, ils regardent tout ce que fait l'homme et ignorent la part surnaturelle d'une plante qui jaillit d'une nouvelle vie. Des scientifiques du monde entier travaillent d'arrache-pied pour intégrer le raisonnement humain dans tout ce qui s'est jamais produit, même la création du monde. Les scientifiques, avec tout leur savoir et leur sagesse, tentent de donner des explications logiques sur les raisons pour lesquelles les catastrophes naturelles et les crises mondiales se produisent. S'ils peuvent tout expliquer, alors ils peuvent écarter Dieu et Son existence. Cela permet à la race humaine d'agir comme bon lui semble sans conséquences éternelles. Cela conduit, à son tour, à un grand sentiment de paix illusoire.

Les humanistes, avec tout leur raisonnement, se moquent de l'existence même de Dieu. Si vous allez dans la plupart des universités en Amérique et que vous parlez aux gens du christianisme, ils se moquent de vous et rient du fait que les chrétiens croient réellement en Dieu.

Le second type de croyance humaniste est une théorie d'humanisme qui reconnaît l'existence de Dieu. Un anthropologue a soutenu que l'humanisme est un projet de la modernité et une continuation sécularisée de la théologie chrétienne occidentale. Mais si vous demandez aux gens ce qu'ils pensent que signifie l'humanisme, vous obtiendrez probablement des réponses différentes, et cela devient très confus. Mais pourquoi cette confusion ? Parce que les gens essaient d'être des humanistes chrétiens. L'humanisme chrétien a fréquemment été critiqué pour son caractère vague et difficile à définir. La raison pour laquelle cela est devenu si confus est que les gens veulent croire en Dieu mais aussi croire en eux-mêmes et que le monde tourne autour d'eux.

Dans les Romains, nous lisons : « Car la colère de Dieu se révèle du ciel contre toute impiété et toute injustice des hommes qui retiennent la vérité captive dans l'injustice ; parce que ce qu'on peut connaître de Dieu leur est manifesté ; car Dieu le leur a manifesté. Les choses invisibles de lui, depuis la création du monde, se voient ; ses éternels attributs, sa puissance et sa divinité, se discernent à l'intelligence dans les choses qu'il a faites, de sorte qu'ils sont inexcusables : parce qu'ayant connu Dieu, ils ne l'ont pas glorifié comme Dieu, et ne lui ont pas rendu grâces, mais se sont égarés dans leurs pensées, et leur cœur insensé s'est obscurci. Se croyant sages, ils sont devenus fous, et ils ont changé la gloire de Dieu incorruptible en images, faites selon l'apparence de l'homme corruptible, et d'oiseaux, et de quadrupèdes, et de reptiles. C'est pourquoi aussi Dieu les a livrés aux convoitises infâmes ; leurs femmes ont changé l'usage naturel en celui qui est contre nature ; et de même aussi les hommes, abandonnant l'usage naturel de la femme, se sont enflammés dans leurs désirs les uns pour les autres, commettant homme avec homme des choses honteuses, et recevant en eux-mêmes la rétribution due à leur égarement. Et puisqu'ils n'ont pas voulu avoir la connaissance de Dieu, Dieu les a livrés à un esprit d'égarement, pour faire ce qui est inconvenant ; remplis de toute injustice, de fornication, de méchanceté, d'avarice, de malice ; pleins d'envie, de meurtre, de querelle, de fraude, de médisance ; calomniateurs, ennemis de Dieu, outrageants, orgueilleux, vaniteux, inventeurs de choses mauvaises, désobéissants aux parents, privés d'entendement, sans alliance, sans affection naturelle, impitoyables, sans miséricorde ; qui, connaissant le jugement de Dieu, que ceux qui font de telles choses sont dignes de mort, non seulement les pratiquent, mais en consentent à ceux qui les commettent. » (Romains 1:18-32).

Alors comment peut-on être humaniste et croire en Dieu ? C'est là que nous touchons un peu plus près de chez nous. Ce type d'humaniste croit que Dieu veut qu'il soit heureux. Il croit en un Dieu Créateur mais ne pense pas qu'il doive Le servir en réalité. Il ne croit pas au vrai Dieu mais, dans son esprit, a créé un dieu fictif qui n'existe pas. Cela lui permet de vivre pour lui-même et pour son propre bonheur. Ce type de personne parlera de Dieu, ira à l'église, chantera des cantiques et dira des prières. Cependant, il ne regardera que vers l'homme pour tous ses besoins. S'il est malade, il appelle un médecin. S'il a besoin d'argent, il va voir le banquier. Si le besoin est une pause dans la réalité, il prend des vacances ou une retraite. Il vit pour son propre bonheur et ensuite remercie Dieu bien qu'il ne se soit pas tourné vers Dieu pour ses besoins. Ces gens dépendent d'eux-mêmes. Ils ont confiance en eux-mêmes.

Voici un exemple : Un chrétien plante un jardin et en prend soin chaque jour. Il arrose, fertilise, désherbe et taille. Finalement, ses plantes commencent toutes à porter du fruit, de beaux fruits. Il remercie Dieu pour la récolte abondante. Son voisin, un humaniste athée, a aussi planté un jardin. Lui aussi sortait chaque jour, arrosait, taillait, désherbait et fertilisait. Il obtint également une récolte abondante. Cet homme, cependant, s'en vanta, attribuant tout ce qu'il avait accompli à lui-même. Les deux hommes ont fait les mêmes choses et ont obtenu des résultats semblables. L'un a rendu gloire à Dieu, l'autre s'est attribué le mérite. Il dira qu'il a accompli la même chose sans Dieu que son voisin a accomplie avec Dieu. Les chrétiens savent qu'il a tort et qu'il avait en réalité besoin de Dieu pour faire croître son jardin.

Lorsqu'il se produit quelque chose qui exige une intervention surnaturelle, l'humaniste chrétien prie et demande aux autres de prier. Cependant, il ne croit pas que Dieu répondra à leurs prières et se met immédiatement au travail pour résoudre son problème, en ne comptant que sur le raisonnement humain. Puis, si le problème est résolu, il remercie Dieu pour cela. Ce type d'humanisme a embrouillé le monde moderne. Il a poussé les incroyants à se moquer de la foi chrétienne et à la qualifier de religion sans pouvoir.

Le chrétien ne croit pas au raisonnement humain. Le chrétien croit que le Dieu des cieux est la raison de tout. « Car c'est en lui qu'ont été créées toutes les choses qui sont dans les cieux et sur la terre, les visibles et les invisibles, trônes, seigneuries, dominations, autorités ; tout a été créé par lui et pour lui » (Colossiens 1:16). Nous ne sommes rien sans Lui, et sans Lui nous ne pouvons rien faire. Le christianisme est l'opposé de l'humanisme. Quand le chrétien accomplit quelque chose de surnaturel, quelque chose que l'humaniste ou l'athée ne peut faire, alors nous avons quelque chose qui confondra les sages.

Quand le voisin voit le chrétien aimer ses ennemis, pardonner à celui qui lui a fait du tort et faire des choses qu'il ne peut pas faire, il commence alors à se demander d'où provenait le pouvoir de faire ces choses. Cela le conduit ensuite au Père. Lorsqu'il n'y a rien de surnaturel que nous accomplissions, il est confus.

Et nous alors ?

Je crains que nous ne tombions dans ce piège de « l'humanisme chrétien ». Nous parlons la langue ; nous disons que nous croyons en Dieu. Nous allons à l'église, chantons des cantiques et récitons des prières. Cependant, à première vue, nous avons confiance en nous-mêmes. Parce que nous avons centré nos vies sur nous-mêmes et notre bien-être, le Dieu des cieux ne nous entend pas. Nos prières ne sont pas exaucées, et le temps passé à genoux est, au mieux, une lutte. Nous faisons les gestes parce que c'est ainsi que nous avons été instruits, mais notre foi repose sur le raisonnement humain.

Il peut être extrêmement difficile de chercher le Seigneur en vivant dans une société humaniste. Une société qui a perfectionné la poursuite de la liberté et du bonheur. Peu à peu, l'Église cède aux façons de ce monde.

Un ministre de Chine visitait les églises en Amérique. Avant de repartir pour la Chine, on lui demanda ce qui l'avait le plus impressionné dans les églises américaines. Il répondit : « Je suis étonné de voir tout ce qu'ils ont accompli sans Dieu. »

Nous ferions bien de simplifier la définition moderne de l'humanisme. L'humaniste nie fièrement qu'il y ait un Dieu lorsqu'il se vante de sa propre force et de ses capacités. Il proclame les grandes réalisations de l'homme et se moque du chrétien humble.

Le chrétien se renie, prend sa croix et suit son Maître. Le chrétien ne pense rien de lui-même ni des capacités de l'homme, avouant avec confiance qu'il n'est que poussière et qu'à cette poussière il retournera rapidement. Le chrétien cherche le bien chez les autres et fait confiance à Dieu pour tous ses besoins et soucis quotidiens.

Les chrétiens croient qu'ils ne sont que des serviteurs de leur maître. Ils sont haïs par le monde et méprisés par la plupart, rejetés. « Si le monde vous hait, sachez qu'il m'a haï avant vous. » (Jean 15:18) Pour eux, cette vie n'est pas la recherche du bonheur. Les choses de ce monde ne les intéressent même pas. Leur joie et leur paix viennent uniquement du service rendu à leur maître, du plaisir de leur Père céleste. Pour le monde, ils sont étranges. Des fous. Pour Dieu, ils sont Ses chers enfants.

Dieu cherche encore aujourd'hui des personnes qui mettront leur confiance en Lui. Il parcourt toute la terre à la recherche de quelqu'un, quelque part, qui mettra de côté le raisonnement humain et le bon sens et obéira à la voix venue du ciel. Dieu veut des hommes de foi qui feront un pas dans le surnaturel, comme Abraham, Moïse, David, et les milliers de croyants qui les ont suivis. Quelqu'un qui se reniera et ce monde et suivra le Sauveur.

Quand cette vie sera finie, les humanistes, qu'ils disent croire en Dieu ou non, périront. Et les chrétiens iront vivre pour toujours dans la gloire.

Humaniste ? Chrétien ? Humaniste chrétien ? Lequel êtes-vous ?

“Dr. Waldron, Elsie needs help!” Elsie’s husband was adamant, almost angry, as he stared at me. On the other hand, Elsie stared at the floor, almost as though she wasn’t present. I had never met either of the couple before and was struggling just a little to figure out what was needed from me to help her.

“What is going on?” I asked as I flipped through her chart. This was still in the days of paper charts, and I headed to the lab section of her chart. There wasn’t anything too crazy that I could see there—her liver enzymes were a little elevated, but otherwise, everything seemed OK.

“It’s her drinking!” Her husband told me. “She is drinking more and more every night. She won’t go out except to get whiskey. She drinks till she passes out every night and has to have something every morning to get her started.”

“Is that true?” I asked Elsie, feeling like a judge overseeing a jury trial.

“Yes,” she said. Her face was emotionless, and I couldn’t tell if she wanted to be there or not.

“Do you want help?” I asked her. This was a loaded question. Many people who struggle with alcoholism aren’t ready to break free from its vice-like hold on them. Maybe Elsie was different.

“I guess so,” she said, indifferently. Once again, I couldn’t tell whether she wanted to be there or not.

“At the rate at which you are drinking, you will kill yourself within a year – maybe two at best – if you don’t give up alcohol entirely,” I told her. “If you want to, I will try to find you an inpatient program to detox you and get you off of alcohol.”

“She’s ready,” he husband said firmly.

When dealing with someone who drinks heavily, it is crucial that they don’t simply stop drinking without medical support. Abrupt cessation of alcohol use causes the body to go into withdrawal which can produce a state called Delirium Tremens and even seizures.

I stepped out of the exam room and to make phone calls. It is never easy to find a place for someone to attempt to rehabilitate from any kind of substances, and it was over an hour and a half before I found a facility that was willing to take Elsie and try to help her get off of the whiskey.

I sighed as I reentered her exam room. I had been afraid that I wouldn’t find anywhere for her to go.

I told them about the plan, and her husband nodded vigorously, while Elise continued to stare silently at the floor. “Can we pray together before you go?” I asked them, and when they nodded assent, I prayed with them, asking for freedom and Jesus’ presence in both of their lives.

They left my office with marching orders and directions on where to go. I had a happy glow about me for the rest of the morning, knowing that I had gone the extra mile and had really made a difference in this middle-aged couple’s life.

Around 2 pm, I got a call from the rehab facility. They hadn’t seen even a shadow of Elsie or her husband, which was surprising, since it was a bright sunny day and the facility wasn’t that far away. With a sinking feeling, I dialed the couple’s phone number.

“She won’t go!” Her husband told me. “She tells me that she told me this ahead of time. She’ll try to cut back, but she isn’t willing to go into a rehab facility or any such thing. I guess just tell them that we’ll let them know if she changes her mind.”

My nurse called the rehab facility and told them the bad news, and I sat down in my chair, stunned. What else could I have done? Was there a solution for Elsie—something different that I could have said that would have made a difference in her life?

About a year later, I received the sad news that Elsie had died at home. I was certain that things would have been different if she had gone to rehab and if she had given control to Jesus. None of that had happened, and I felt cynicism pushing into my heart.

Cynicism

We live in an age of cynicism. In ancient Greece, the cynics were an odd assortment of men who specialized in being grouchy and saying mean (they would have said truthful) things to people. They often dressed in rags and behaved in such a way that most of the polite Athenians did not want to be close to them.

Today, cynicism means a tendency to believe the worst about people and circumstances. Cynical people believe that all people are motivated purely by selfishness and that bad events will tend to prevail.

Many young doctors are idealistic and very hopeful. They believe that if they exert the utmost effort, they can make a real, positive impact on their patient’s lives. Unfortunately, as time goes by and they try their hardest and their patients don’t change, they can give up. These doctors still try, but they no longer really hope that their efforts will make much of a difference.

It seems as though people who get involved with politics often have the best of intentions. They see this as a path to changing society for the better. Unfortunately, as time goes by and the faces in charge change, the policies don’t really change, they tend to become cynical.

Sometimes this cynicism is directed against all politicians. Sometimes it is only anger directed against members of the party that opposes their party’s positions. Hope is replaced by cynicism.

Cynicism in the Bible

If there is a book in the Bible that seems to have been written by a cynical man, it is the book of Ecclesiastes. The Preacher, who we understand to be Solomon, lists all of the things that he endeavored in an attempt to find joy.

In chapter 2:17-23 Solomon describes work as futile. He finishes by saying, “For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun? For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity.” (Ecclesiastes 2:22,23)

He saw the world as being dominated by tyrants and there was little that the people could do about it. Solomon went so far as to say that political power was meaningless “Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished. For out of prison he cometh to reign; whereas also he that is born in his kingdom becometh poor” (Ecclesiastes 4:13).

In Ecclesiastes 6:6, he seems to disparage long life. “Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?”

Of course, he finishes his short book with the instruction to remember our Creator in the days of our youth. There is a blessing for those who choose to focus on God when they have a little bit of energy left and not, when they are old and jaded, like Solomon.

Later on, it almost seemed as though God had given up on His people. He still sent prophets to them, but He knew without a doubt that the people would refuse to respond. “Therefore thou shalt speak all these words unto them; but they will not hearken to thee: thou shalt also call unto them; but they will not answer thee” (Jeremiah 7:27).

Even in the New Testament, Paul told Timothy that the time was coming when people would no longer listen to sound doctrine. “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;” (2 Timothy 4:3).

By picking and choosing these passages, we can come away with a very gloomy view of the future and, more specifically, of human’s willingness to change. It seems there is little point of investing ourselves in the people around us. They are full of woe and are as likely to change as a chipmunk is to master differential calculus.

The Opposite of Cynicism

The opposite of cynicism is hope. It is the belief that the future could be better.

It is interesting that the Apostle Paul spoke of tribulations in the Epistle to the Romans, “And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope: and hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us” (Romans 5:3-5).

We may not have reached the place where we glory in the trials we experience, but certainly, they should bring us these other things that he mentions. For, we grow in patience and experience, even as we deal with trials, but more than that, we come to realize that we have hope for tomorrow because we serve a great God.

The contrast in the story of the Prodigal Son in Luke 15 teaches us much about hope. The father and the older brother were strikingly different in their attitudes.

The father had never given up hope – he knew that his son had failed him and gone far from what he knew was right and yet, the father still desired to see the prodigal come to himself and return home.

On the other hand, the older brother not only had no hope for his younger brother, but he was also angry with him. The prodigal had wasted his money, he had lived in sin, and now, he had returned home just because he was out of money.

Certainly, there was no reason to trust the younger son. Yet, that is exactly what our Heavenly Father does for us.

Look for Hope in the Right Places

Part of the problem is that we look for hope in the wrong places. A number of years ago, a presidential candidate ran for office under the slogan “Hope and Change,” and yet, even though he was elected, I imagine most folks did not feel that their lives were significantly changed for the better.

Pursuing the things this world values—political power and wealth is guaranteed to bring emptiness. This is Satan’s pattern—he always over-promises and under-delivers.

This was what he did when he tempted Jesus, “All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:8). All of the things Satan offered, nothing compared with the glory that Jesus eventually received from the road that led to the cross.

In the same way, Satan would like to distract Christians from seeking the things that are valuable, and that will bring hope. Satan tells Christians that politics will not only change the world for the better, it is an easier way to change the world.

The Bible is clear that we build hope as we nurture our relationship with God and then work to help our brothers and sisters build that same relationship in their own lives. The reason that we can hope is not because people are so wonderful—we don’t have to live very long to realize that they aren’t. The reason we hope is because we serve an awesome, faithful God who walks with us through the worst of our trials.

Remember that We Have Undeserved Hope

Jesus’ messages about forgiveness make it clear that one of the major reasons that we have for forgiving others in our lives is that we have received great and undeserved forgiveness. The same is true for hope.

Each one of us was hopeless and without reason to expect to receive hope and we were still given a ray of light in the midst of our darkness. Maybe part of the reason that we have so much trouble hoping for good things for the people around us is that we do not remember how hopeless we were before we found grace.

If Jesus was able to bring hope to our hopeless existence, then certainly He can do wonderful things in the hearts and lives of others around us. The only people we should give up on are the ones that our Savior has given up on as well.

Small Efforts Do Make a Difference

I remember having a conversation with a young person who was planning to go into medicine and had a plan to go to a foreign country and serve the people there. As we were talking, an older man entered the conversation and shared that he saw little hope for change in developing countries.

The people in those countries just weren’t interested in getting better and didn’t do the minimum necessary to stave off things like worms and parasites. Doctors and nurses couldn’t make a difference in such an environment.

I could sense the heart of the youth sinking as this older man shared. He had experience, and he had given up hope. The sad thing was that he was also stealing the hope of someone who still had a desire to serve.

When I was in training, I had a surgeon tell me that family doctors didn’t really do anything. They simply kept their patients alive till their next office visit, whereas surgeons really “fixed” people—taking out (or off) the offending body part.

At the end of the day, small efforts do make a difference. I don’t do brain surgery, but I still can make a difference in someone else’s life— maybe just by spending a little time and listening and praying. This is true for all of us.

More than that, we come to realize that making this effort changes our own lives for the better. Jesus told the sheep that as they ministered to “the least of these my brethren,” they were ministering to Him.

Even if no one’s life is improved, our Savior knows our desires and feels our efforts, and will reward them someday.

A Few Things to Remember

When we face failures, we tend to move in one of two directions. Those of us who are optimists tend to believe that this episode was an isolated event and that the future is still bright. On the other hand, pessimists believe that failures are permanent, personal, and pervasive.

Pessimists believe that their failures are the result of intrinsic character flaws that they have and that these things affect all of their lives and are unlikely to change. Unlike the righteous man who falls to rise again, these people fall and lie where they fall, defeated at the outset.

When we are dealing with other people, we need to give them the same grace that we should give ourselves. They, too, are growing, and if they have a failure today, they will do better tomorrow. Maybe they will fail again, but they will at least “fail better.”

Conclusion

Cynicism is rife in our world. Many have given up hope for a better future, and it is understandable for those who have invested their hope in this world’s institutions. There is no real hope in government or in armies or in bureaucracy.

The song says, “Oh to have no hope in Jesus, how dark this world must be!” For, Jesus is the one who brings light into our darkness and allows us to continue, even when others fail us.

God is the one who redeems us. He is the one who sent the prophets, even though their messages were ignored, and the prophets were persecuted. He is the one who continues to hope for us, even when we have failed Him so many times in the past.

He is the reason we carry on. He is the reason that we have hope, not only for ourselves but also for our brothers.
